title: New drought support for farmers

content.content: Today, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, and Farming Minister, Stephen Morgan, have announced a package of support to help farmers manage the impacts of this summer’s extreme dry weather. The announcement was made during their visit to a farm in Cornwall.

Heatwaves and below-average rainfall have increased pressure on water resources for agricultural production and Environmental Land Management (ELM) scheme activities. Dry conditions and heat have also increased the risk of wildfires across many parts of the country.
We know these conditions are creating real challenges for farmers.
On Wednesday, the Prime Minister chaired the government’s emergency response committee (COBR) on extreme heat, wildfires and drought.
Following COBR, measures announced today will help farmers manage drought pressures, protect crops and strengthen resilience for the future.
We’ve confirmed:
Our investment today supports our Farming Roadmap vision of building a stronger, more resilient farming sector.

We're committed to working with farmers to improve the resilience of on-farm water supplies. This includes making sure the right planning and abstraction licensing arrangements are in place so farmers can invest with confidence.
We'll continue to monitor the situation closely and work with the farming and water sectors. If needed, we'll take further action to help farmers manage the impacts of drought.
In this post, we explain the support announced today, who is eligible, and how farmers can benefit.
ELM temporary adjustments
We're introducing temporary adjustments to our ELM schemes to give farm businesses flexibility where prolonged dry weather is affecting their ability to meet agreement requirements.
To help farmers manage the impacts, we're:
Using temporary adjustments will not affect the payments you receive under your ELM agreement.
Read the full guidance on GOV.UK.
Eligibility
These temporary adjustments apply to ELM revenue agreements under the following schemes:
You can use a temporary adjustment if your land is in a county where the Environment Agency has declared ‘drought’ or ‘prolonged dry weather’ status.
As of 15 August 2026, all counties in England meet this criteria, meaning that all ELM agreement holders can use the temporary adjustments.
The temporary adjustments will remain available until the Environment Agency returns the county to normal status.
Keep up to date
You can check the latest drought status through Environment Agency drought reports.
The RPA keeps extreme weather guidance for farmers and land managers up to date on GOV.UK.
Earlier this week, we published a blog post rounding up information and resources to help farmers and growers manage farms and land during drought.
£50m increase to SFI Window 2
We're increasing funding for SFI26 Window 2 by £50m.

This takes the total SFI26 budget to £290m for new agreements. The additional funding will help more farmers access a reliable income stream at a time when many are facing lower yields and rising costs.
This will help more farmers sustainably manage soils, livestock, nutrients, fertiliser use and farm wildlife alongside food production.
SFI already funds drought-resilient, sustainable farming practices like increasing soil organic matter levels in arable soils through cover crops, and minimising soil disturbance through no-till.
Many of these actions improve soil health and increases the land’s ability to retain moisture, helping farmers manage the immediate weather while also increasing resilience for the future.
Window 2 will open in September to all farmers.
Earlier this month we published an update on SFI26, including details about how to apply. We will monitor demand for the scheme closely as applications open.
Water Management Grant
We're reopening the Water Management Grant, with up to £15m available to help farmers build on-farm reservoirs.
The grant is expected to open in the autumn.
This means that farmers will be able to store more water when it’s available and use it when it is needed most, improving resilience during dry periods and helping protect crop production.

On-farm water storage is an important part of preparing for more frequent periods of extreme weather. Having access to a reliable supply of water can help farmers manage short-term pressures while strengthening the long-term resilience of their businesses.
The scheme will focus on supporting water storage for crop irrigation, helping the horticulture and arable sectors adapt to climate change and improve resilience to drought.
If demand exceeds the funding available, we will keep the budget under review and consider providing additional funding.

Government has already announced plans to support the development of nine new reservoirs, to strengthen the country's water infrastructure and improve resilience to future droughts, floods and extreme weather.
Reducing planning barriers to building reservoirs
We're making it easier for farmers to build on-farm reservoirs.

Next week, we will publish our response to the National Planning Policy Framework consultation, making it clear that local authorities should support the development of agricultural infrastructure, including reservoirs.
This also means boosting support for greenhouses, polytunnels and farm shops – infrastructure that's essential for modern, productive farming.

In September, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) will publish updated planning guidance for on-farm reservoirs to give farmers more clarity and confidence when investing in water resilience.

Defra and MHCLG will work with farmers and industry representatives, including the NFU and CLA, to review evidence on the effectiveness of current permitted development rights (PDRs) for on-farm reservoirs.
This is a first step in considering whether further planning reforms are needed to support the delivery of the infrastructure required for food production.
Environment Agency Regulatory Flexibilities
If you hold an abstraction licence and are concerned about your water supply, contact the Environment Agency as early as possible.
Farmers can already apply for temporary flexibilities from the Environment Agency to help access water during periods of extreme dry weather.
These flexibilities can include:
All requests are assessed carefully to consider the impact on the environment or other water users.
We know that we need to get abstraction licensing right so that investment in a reservoir makes sense for farmers.

From September, the Environment Agency is simplifying its application process for long-duration abstraction licences for reservoirs. This will make it easier for farmers and other abstractors to apply for licences that better support long-term investment in water storage and resilience, and help farmers secure long-term finance.
Subscribe to the Farming Blog
Subscribe to the Farming Blog to stay up to date with news about funding. You'll receive a notification as soon as any new information is available.

title: What is HPV and how effective is the vaccine that protects against it?

content.content: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a very common viral infection. Here's what you need to know, including the remarkable story of how a vaccine is helping to eliminate some cancers caused by HPV entirely.
What is HPV?

There are more than 100 types of HPV. The virus affects the skin and mucous membranes - places like the mouth, throat, vagina, and anus. Most people will encounter some type of HPV during their lifetime. The vast majority who catch the infection will never know, because for most people it causes no symptoms and clears on its own.

However, some strains are more concerning. Certain ‘high-risk’ types of HPV can cause abnormal cell changes that, over time, may develop into cancer. These include cervical cancer, anal cancer, penile cancer, vulval and vaginal cancer, and some cancers of the mouth and throat. Low-risk types - while not linked to cancer – can cause genital warts.

HPV spreads through skin-to-skin contact, most commonly during sexual activity. You do not need to have penetrative sex to contract it, and you can get it the very first time you're sexually active. Condoms offer some protection, but because they don't cover all the skin around the genitals, they cannot eliminate the risk entirely.
How effective is the vaccine?

The HPV vaccine used in the UK is Gardasil 9, which protects against 9 types of the virus. These include types 16 and 18 - responsible for around 75% of all cervical cancers - as well as 5 additional high-risk types. The vaccine also protects against types 6 and 11, which cause roughly 90% of genital warts.

Since the vaccine was introduced, rates of cervical cancer and genital warts among young people have fallen dramatically. Research published in the Lancet found that there were no deaths from cervical cancer between 2020 and 2024 among women aged 20 to 24 who had received the HPV vaccine at school. Vaccine coverage in this cohort was around 88% to 90%. Based on historical rates, 23 deaths would have been expected during this period, representing a 100% reduction in mortality.

Earlier cohorts, vaccinated with slightly lower coverage, also saw dramatic reductions - 80% fewer deaths in some age groups. In total, HPV vaccination in England is estimated to have prevented around 200 cervical cancer deaths up to the end of 2024.

This is genuinely historic. A vaccine is, for practical purposes, eliminating deaths from cervical cancer in young women. But we cannot afford to be complacent. In recent years uptake rates for HPV vaccination among girls and boys have fallen compared to rates seen before the pandemic, and we know that there are variations in the proportion of young people taking up the vaccine depending on where they are and the circumstances in which they live. There is a risk of growing numbers of young people missing out on the vital protection that the HPV vaccine provides.

Importantly, even if you have been vaccinated, you should still attend cervical screening appointments if you are eligible. The vaccine does not protect against all types of HPV, so screening remains an important safety net and one of the best ways to protect yourself from cervical cancer.
Who can have the vaccine?
The HPV vaccine is recommended and available free on the NHS to several groups:
Most people who are eligible can have the vaccine. The only people who cannot are those who have previously had a serious allergic reaction to a dose of the vaccine or one of its ingredients.
Younger people typically need just one dose, while those aged 25 to 45 usually need 2 doses given several months apart. People with a weakened immune system may require 3 doses.
What are the side effects of the HPV vaccine?

Side effects from the HPV vaccine are generally mild and short-lived. The most common ones are soreness, swelling, or redness where the injection was given - the kind of reaction many people experience with any vaccine. Some people also report a headache, mild fever, dizziness, nausea, or tiredness in the day or two after their dose.

Serious side effects are very rare. As with all vaccines, there is a small risk of a severe allergic reaction, but the healthcare professionals administering the vaccine are trained to recognise and treat this immediately.
A generation protected

The HPV vaccine represents one of the great success stories of modern public health. If you're unsure whether you or someone in your family is up to date, speak to your GP or visit a sexual health clinic.

title: National rollout of Photos at Test

content.content: Earlier this year we completed phase 2 of the MOT Photos at Test trial, formerly known as Images in Garages. Phase 2 of the trial was really important because it showed that we’d progressed to a point where national rollout is now possible.
Why we’re introducing photos at test
Although rare, MOT fraud compromises road safety and damages the reputation of hard working MOT testers across the country.

Results of the trials
Across phases 1 and 2 of the trials, over 300 garages took part, uploading over 60,000 images to MTS with a 92% success rate.
The trials also demonstrated that the feature had minimal impact on testing times, with initial tests remaining at around 40 minutes and retests only slightly longer.
We were also pleased to see that 88% those involved in the trial were ‘very satisfied’ or ‘satisfied’ with how easy the new feature was to use.
Overall, the trials were a success and demonstrated how well testers adapted to including a photo of the vehicle being tested in the testing bay.
Next steps
On 3 August 2026, the national rollout began and an additional 2,500 garages across Great Britain received access to the feature.
Over time we will provide access to more garages until all MOT testers have access to upload photos.
We’d recommend using the new feature once it becomes available to your garage. Familiarise yourself with how it works, as it may become mandatory in future.

title: Why exam results season should inspire employers, by Phil Smith

content.content: Thousands of young people receiving their exam results will be weighing up their next steps.
Whatever grades they achieve, one thing I’m sure we would all agree on is that they deserve the best possible chance of success in their lives and careers.
We need our young people to feel optimistic and there will be lots of hope for the future among those finding out how they did in their A Levels, T Levels and GCSEs.
Sadly, there will be some trepidation too – not just about how well or otherwise they may have done in these exams, but over their longer-term prospects.
The struggles of young people not in education, employment, or training have been well documented through Alan Milburn’s review of the NEETs problem faced by this country.

His recent report warned that nearly 1 million young people in the UK are NEET. The government is addressing this through the Youth Guarantee of training, work experience, or placement opportunities for young people. This includes the creation of 300,000 new work experience and training placements in sectors like construction, health and social care and hospitality.

Skills England is determined to play our part too. We’ve worked with businesses, training providers and other partners over the past year to make sure skills training, for our emerging workforce, is high quality and responsive to the needs of a modern economy. This has included the rollout of new programmes such as the Level 4 AI and Automation Practitioner apprenticeship, alongside flexible apprenticeship units focused on AI leadership and strategy.
A key priority for everyone is redressing a 40% decline in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.
We used to hear concerns about whether young people wanted apprenticeships. The reality is now the opposite.

On average, there are more than ten applicants for every vacancy advertised through the government’s Find An Apprenticeship service, with many high-profile companies receiving thousands of applications for their programmes.
So, demand is vastly outstripping supply and we need many more large and small businesses to invest in apprenticeships.
For me, it’s a no-brainer. Once you get past the hump of worrying about how to sign up – through a process we are helping to simplify – then you see fast returns.
Skilled staff are more productive – the estimated yearly gain for businesses can be as much as £18,000 per apprentice.

I saw first-hand, when I ran Cisco UK and Ireland, how investing in young people re-invigorated our workforce. Their energy, fresh perspectives and willingness to learn was infectious. Apprenticeships also provide the opportunity to embed people into your company culture, which we found fostered a lot of loyalty.

T Level students will be getting their results on Thursday, 13 August. A big reason why these qualifications have bedded in well, since their launch six years ago, has been the substantial work experience involved.
They offer a mixture of classroom learning and ‘on-the-job’ experience during an industry placement of at least 315 hours (approximately 45 days).

Offering these placements is another excellent way for businesses to refresh their workforce. Around a quarter of students, who progress from T Levels into work, get their jobs with their industry placement employer.
For example, Lloyds Banking Group has been a long-term supporter of T Level, growing from providing six placements in 2022 to more than 100 annually over the past three years.

Around half of their placement students have progressed into permanent roles. John Banks, their T Levels manager, reflected that this has helped Lloyds build a workforce which “better reflects the communities we serve and creates opportunities for talented young people who may not have considered a career with us otherwise”.
Skills training is really good for business and Britain has no shortage of enthusiastic and talented young people and I'd like to congratulate all those collecting their results.
But I would also like to take this opportunity to invite many more employers to draw inspiration from all the optimism surrounding exam results and check out how to invest in young people today.

title: Why water regulation is changing – and how Clear Waters is helping

content.content: Regulating the environmental performance of the water industry is a core Environment Agency function. Since 2023 we have been transforming the way we regulate the water industry. Backed by significant investment we are delivering increased scrutiny and oversight through a specialised workforce dedicated to each water and sewerage company.

We recognise that further change is needed and that improvements need to be delivered at pace. We are working with government and partners to support thriving places, communities and sustainable growth while protecting and improving the environment.
A sector under scrutiny

It's our job to help protect homes and habitats, including England's water environment. We know how important rivers, lakes and coastal waters are to people and that they rightly want to see faster improvement and greater investment to better protect them.
That’s why transparency and accountability are more important than ever - so that people can see and understand what is happening in the places they live, work and spend time.

The Environment Agency is committed to transparency. Making our data accessible to the public is key to this. For example, we have already worked with Ofwat to develop an interactive map that shows where the water industry investment is being made at a local level to protect and improve the environment: Price Review 2024 Water Industry National Environment Programme (WINEP) App.
Introducing Clear Waters

Clear Waters is a further extension of this work – a collaborative project to make information about water company environmental investment more transparent, accessible and useful. The Clear Waters group brings together regulators, environmental groups, the water sector, local authority representatives and consumer groups. The partnership is developing a shared approach to showing what environmental improvements are planned, where they are being delivered and how progress can be tracked. The aim is to help customers and stakeholders understand not just how much is being invested, but what that investment will deliver for rivers, lakes, groundwater and coastal waters in places they care about.
Addressing the transparency gap
By making environmental commitments visible and measurable, Clear Waters will support greater scrutiny of progress on delivery and help to rebuild public trust.

Clear Waters is already making progress: by working directly with customers and users of water-related information, the project has produced user profiles that are now being used to shape how water industry investment information is presented. This will make it easier for people to find , understand and use information about environmental investment and outcomes. Any lessons learned from this will then help inform how information on future investment is shared and accessed, ensuring it is more relevant, accessible and meaningful to the people who use it.

Clear Waters is already helping to bring together people with different perspectives on water and environmental data. At Northumbrian Water's Innovation Festival in July, representatives from regulators, water companies, environmental organisations, academia and technology organisations explored how information can be made easier to access, understand and use. Discussions focused on making environmental data more meaningful for different audiences, improving transparency around environmental outcomes and exploring how citizen science can complement existing monitoring.
Shaping the future of water regulation

Clear Waters will also play a key role in the transition to a new single regulator as set out in the Government's White Paper in January 2026. Lessons learned through our work will feed into thinking for future investment programmes, helping to shape a stronger, more accountable system for the future.

As well as the Clear Waters project, the Environment Agency is also working with Ofwat, the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural England and Natural Resources Wales on a joint programme of improvements to how we deliver water regulation and delivering meaningful change now, rather than waiting for policy or legislative change.

Insights from Clear Waters will help shape future approaches to transparency and public engagement, supporting preparations for future investment programmes and helping ensure investment decisions are understood by the people and communities they are intended to benefit.
What’s next for Clear Waters?

The partnership will continue to develop and test new ways to help people better understand environmental improvements and track progress over time. Priorities include improving access to information, exploring how different sources of environmental data can be used together, and ensuring information is presented in ways that meet the needs of different audiences.
Get involved
The Clear Waters partnership is planning activity over the autumn. If you'd like to be involved, please contact clearwaters@ofwat.gov.uk.

title: Results day 2026: What's next after picking up your A level, T Level and VTQ results?

content.content: It can feel like there’s a lot riding on A Level, T Level and Vocational Technical Qualifications (VTQ) results day but if you don’t get your predicted grades, don’t worry - it doesn’t mean that your education journey stops here.
It's also important to remember that the number of top grades has no bearing on the number of university places available.

Even if you don’t get exactly the grades you’d expected, you may be able to follow the route you were preparing to take. But if you do need to change your plans, there are plenty of alternative, exciting options for everyone.
Here we explain your choices if things didn’t go to plan on results day.
When is A level/T Level/VTQ results day 2026?
Results day this year is on Thursday 13 August 2026.
What if I don’t get the grades I need for my university course?
Even if you don’t get the grades you need, your university or college may still offer you a place.
Whatever your grades, there’s still time to rethink your plans if you’re having second thoughts. And if you didn’t make your university offer, there are plenty of alternative options out there.
The first thing you should do is talk to your school or college, and to your preferred university or college, as they may be able to offer some flexibility.
University admissions teams will be on hand on results day to help students and have plenty of experience with helping applicants to find a course that will allow them thrive.
Find your university’s admissions contact details by heading to the admission section of their website.
What if I don’t pass all the components of my T Level?
Don’t worry if you haven’t passed all the components of your T Level – you may still be able to secure enough UCAS points to go to university, if that’s your plan
UCAS points are available for those who have completed their industry placement and passed either the core or occupational specialism part of their T Level.
How many UCAS points you achieve will vary depending on the T Level subject you took as the weighting of the core and occupational specialism for each course varies.
You can find out how many UCAS points you can achieve for only partially passing your T Level with the UCAS tariff calculator.
What are my options if I still want to go to university or continue studying?
Clearing

Clearing is when UCAS provides students with the chance to apply for university places which haven’t yet been filled. It’s available to anyone who has made a UCAS Undergraduate application and doesn’t hold any offers.
Clearing provides an opportunity for those who have missed their conditions or had a last-minute change of heart about the university or course they want to study.
How do I know if I’m eligible to find a course through clearing?
Clearing runs from 2 July until 19 October 2026. You will be eligible if:
You can find out more about clearing by watching this video from UCAS.
Resit
If you’re unhappy with your results you can apply to  resit your subjects in summer 2027.
You should speak to your school or college about retaking exams.
Higher Technical Qualifications (HTQs)
If you’re interested in continuing your education but an undergraduate degree isn’t for you, then you might want to consider a HTQ.
HTQs are technical qualifications that employers have helped develop so you can get the tailored training and skills you need to secure a job in your chosen industry.
You can study a HTQ full time or part time. You’re usually taught in a classroom at a college, university or an independent training provider.
You can take a HTQ in a variety of different subjects across a wide range of sectors, including healthcare, digital, construction, engineering and education.
You also may be eligible for student finance. The amount you could get will depend on your circumstances and the type of HTQ you’re studying. You can find a HTQ through UCAS.
Apprenticeships
There are now more than 700 high quality apprenticeships in a wide range of roles.
This includes high level apprenticeships, like degree apprenticeships in nursing, engineering, law, and science.
Apprentices earn while learning, gaining valuable on-the-job experience while receiving training at university or college.
You can search for apprenticeships here.
School leaver scheme
Some companies offer school leaver schemes to young people who have completed A levels. The schemes allow young people to learn and train with a large company while earning a wage.
School leaver schemes are usually like graduate schemes, except they’re aimed at pupils who’ve recently left school. You can apply to the scheme while you’re still in school.
Employers create their own schemes, so students need to search for school leaver schemes or check each company’s website to see if one is available and apply.
What if I’m not sure what I want to do?
Talk to a National Careers Service adviser

Whatever your results, you have lots of options and there is more than one route into most careers. It’s not always grades which are the most important thing, and employers look for a range of skills and qualifications.

First of all, you should talk to your school or college to discuss your options. Friends and family can also be a source of support to bounce ideas off, but it can be useful to talk your plans through with an impartial expert.
You can speak to a professional careers adviser for free and get judgment-free, confidential information and advice via the National Careers Service Exam Results helpline, via phone or by webchat.
Whatever your results, if you want to find out more about all your education and training options, as well as get practical advice about your exam results, visit the Skills for Careers.
What if I think there’s something wrong with my results?
Speak to your school or college for advice
There is a rigorous system in place which makes sure that exams are marked fairly and accurately.
If you think there has been a mistake in how your exam was marked, you should speak to your school or college who can request a review from the exam board.

You shouldn’t request a review unless you think there has been an error, or you could risk missing out on other options. Consider carefully if appealing is the right course of action for you by discussing it with your school or college.

title: Heatwaves, temperature control and veterinary medicines: how to transport medicines safely

content.content: VMD Voices: Our Experts Explain

With UK summer heatwaves once again putting temperature control in the spotlight, this second blog from VMD inspector, Julia Pearce, follows our earlier advice on storing veterinary medicines safely by looking at how to protect medicines when they are being transported.

In this two-part blog, Julia Pearce explains what VMD inspectors expect to see and shares practical advice to help veterinary practices and authorised retail premises stay compliant with the law - temperature control of veterinary medicines is no longer just good practice, it is a legal requirement.
Credit: Pexels

All too often, inspectors find that temperature monitoring and recording in practice vehicles is either absent or wholly inadequate. In some cases, recorded temperatures are so far outside the acceptable range that there is no reliable assurance the veterinary medicines stored in the vehicle remain safe or effective.

You should research, test and validate your vehicle cold chain storage before use. We are not expecting records covering a full 24‑hour period unless medicines are stored in the vehicle for that length of time. However, you must not place products into storage units until the required temperature range has been reached. You should keep detailed records to show:

You should also test and monitor ambient storage within vehicles. Vehicle temperatures can increase rapidly, particularly on sunny days, even in the absence of extreme weather or a heatwave. Storage conditions within vehicles must therefore be suitable for all veterinary medicines being transported, including for home visits and farm or yard visits.

Where there is a risk that ambient vehicle temperatures may exceed 25°C, you must consider alternative storage solutions, such as validated insulated containers or active cooling systems, to ensure medicines remain within their required storage conditions throughout transport.
Delivering and posting veterinary medicines

Temperature monitoring and recording requirements also apply to all veterinary medicinal products being delivered or dispatched. This includes medicines transported in your own delivery vehicles as well as those sent via courier services. You must be able to demonstrate that appropriate storage conditions are maintained throughout the delivery process, from dispatch to delivery.

You must hold robust records demonstrating that appropriate storage conditions are maintained throughout the delivery process. This applies whether deliveries are carried out using your own vehicles or via a courier service.

Where you do not use your own delivery vehicles, this evidence can be generated using validated “test” parcels. These test parcels must be sent through the courier service under normal delivery conditions. Simply placing a packaged parcel containing a thermometer in a room or storage area for a period of time does not constitute a valid test.

You should carry out testing at least twice a year, and ideally during periods of very cold and very warm weather, to reflect the conditions most likely to challenge your packaging and delivery processes. A risk assessment of the delivery routes and methods must be performed to identify the highest risk routes/customers and these should be used to validate delivery.
The data collected must clearly demonstrate:
This evidence allows you to show inspectors that medicines remain safe, effective, and compliant from dispatch through to delivery.

It is important to be aware that not all courier companies operate to the same standards. Some courier services can provide formal assurances that veterinary medicinal products will be transported in accordance with the required storage conditions. Where such assurances are relied upon, they should be documented, understood, and supported by appropriate evidence.

Ultimately, responsibility for ensuring that veterinary medicines are transported under suitable conditions remains with the supplying premises, and courier services should be selected with this responsibility in mind.
If you would like to discuss storage requirements in more detail please contact the VMD who will put you in touch with your local inspector.
Credit: Unsplash
What about in-post boxes?

If you use a delivery service that deposits parcels in collection boxes rather than delivering directly to a customer’s home address, this must be fully considered as part of your temperature validation and risk assessment.

You must be able to demonstrate that your packaging will maintain the required storage conditions until the point at which the customer takes possession of the product. This requires a clear understanding of:

These variables must be reflected in your validation testing. Practices should carefully assess whether the risks associated with collection box deliveries are acceptable and whether they can be adequately mitigated. In some cases, the safest option may be not to use this delivery method at all.
Protecting medicines from humidity

Humidity must also be considered as part of your storage risk assessment. Unless packaging is specifically designed to withstand moisture and condensation, excessive humidity can cause it to deteriorate to the point where the product is no longer suitable for supply.

If ambient storage areas become too cold, particularly in vehicles, condensation may form on or within packaging. This can damage cartons, labels, and inserts, potentially resulting in the loss of critical product information, including batch numbers and expiry dates.

Where packaging integrity or essential labelling information is compromised, the veterinary medicinal product may no longer be compliant for supply, even if the medicine itself has not been visibly affected.
Canva design
Small issues can have a big impact

As inspectors, we often see temperature records completed diligently every day, even though they clearly show temperatures outside the required range. In some cases, staff have noticed a problem but were unsure what action to take.

Where a refrigerator is operating outside the required temperature range, it is likely that most, if not all, of the veterinary medicines stored within it are no longer safe or efficacious. The consequence can be significant, including the need to dispose of and replace large quantities of stock, often at considerable cost.

A similar issue is frequently seen with vehicle temperature records, where temperatures recorded in the boot of a car have exceeded 30°C for days at a time, yet no action has been taken to protect the veterinary medicines being transported or to assess whether those products remain safe to use.

Recording temperatures alone is not enough. If a temperature excursion occurs, you need to investigate it. Consider whether the thermometer is working correctly, whether equipment has developed a fault, and how long medicines may have been exposed to unsuitable temperatures.
What to do if you think a medicine has been affected by a change in temperature
Where there is any doubt about product integrity, contact the manufacturer early and follow their advice regarding continued use or disposal.

Products showing visible signs of deterioration should be disposed of safely. Vaccines are particularly sensitive to temperature excursions and more often than not are unusable if frozen or exposed to temperatures in excess of 8°C but always remember to check with the manufacturer if you are unsure.

As inspectors, we discuss medicines storage and record keeping with practices during almost every inspection. We know that veterinary teams are incredibly busy, and we want inspections to be a positive opportunity to share advice and support, not just assess compliance.

We hope these practical tips will help make medicines management simpler for your practice or business, support compliance with the Veterinary Medicines Regulations (VMRs), and help ensure that the medicines you supply and use remain safe and effective.

title: Heatwaves, temperature control and veterinary medicines: how to store medicines safely

content.content: VMD Voices: Our Experts Explain

With the UK experiencing summer heatwaves in 2026, it’s important that vet practices and retailers are checking how veterinary medicines are stored and temperatures monitored. High temperatures can increase the risk of medicines being kept outside their required storage conditions, but good temperature control is not just a summer concern. VMD inspectors see storage, monitoring and record-keeping issues all year round, in all types of weather. In this two-part blog, Julia Pearce explains what VMD inspectors expect to see and shares practical advice to help veterinary practices and authorised retail premises stay compliant with the law - temperature control of veterinary medicines is no longer just good practice, it is a legal requirement.
Schedule 3 Paragraph 3E of the Veterinary Medicines Regulations
Retail storage of veterinary medicinal products

This requirement came into effect on 17 May 2024, as part of the 2024 amendments to the 2013 regulations. This applies to any premises that store or transport medicines in all categories, POM-V, POM-VPS, NFA-VPS and AVM-GSL. From temperature monitoring, record keeping and cold chain management to protecting products from light, preventing contamination, and ensuring medicines remain within specification during transport, these blogs provide practical guidance to help you meet these legal obligations.
About the author

I have been at the VMD for 10 years and have previously owned and run a saddlery and pet supplies store for nearly 20 years. I qualified as an SQP in 1994 and have inspected hundreds of vet practices over the years.
Why is temperature control so important

As described in our previous blog on shelf-life and expiry dates, veterinary medicines can degrade from exposure to heat, light, moisture or air. This is why storing medicines at the correct temperature is essential to keep the medicines work as intended.
Credit: Pixabay

During inspections, we ask for evidence that you store veterinary medicines correctly in every location where you keep them. Wherever you store veterinary medicines, you must also have an appropriate temperature monitoring device in place.
What should you expect during an inspection?

Inspectors commonly see temperature records for cold chain products; however, you must now also provide records that show you maintain ambient storage conditions within the required temperature range.

In addition, if you transport veterinary medicines in any capacity, whether for deliveries, by vets visiting clients away from the practice premises, or when moving medicines between a main branch and a smaller branch, you must show that you maintain appropriate storage conditions throughout transport, including within vehicles. This is explored further in the second blog of  two-this two-part series.
How does light affect veterinary medicines?
Credit: Pixabay

When storing veterinary medicines, temperature is not the only consideration. You must also protect some products from light, including artificial light unless the label specifically states direct sunlight only. Always check the product label for storage instructions.
A common example is Calciject No.5 40 CM, which must be protected from light but is often stored on open shelves in veterinary practices and authorised retailers.

A dark-coloured container does not always indicate light protection, and you should not rely on bottle colour alone. If in doubt, keep products in their original packaging and store them in cupboards, cabinets with solid doors, or areas with limited light exposure. You must also protect products that require light protection during transport as well as while storing them in the dispensary.
What temperature should medicines be stored at?

You must store cold chain products between 2°C and 8°C, while most ambient products should stay below 25°C. We also recommend avoiding ambient storage below 12°C, as this is close to the dew point in many indoor environments. If products become colder than the surrounding air, condensation can form, potentially damaging packaging and making labels difficult to read and can encourage mould growth.

Ambient storage areas have some form of climate control to minimise temperature extremes, if not provisions must be implemented to ensure that products are not exposed to temperatures outside those stated on the Summary of Product Characteristics.

Using fans to create airflow can help but during periods of high temperature you must consider your storage locations, Heat rises so higher shelves and storage under skylights or next to windows should be avoided.

For static enclosed locations such as controlled drugs cabinets then the inclusion of a frozen ice pack wrapped in bubble wrap or a towel can lower the temperature in the cabinet, and the wrapping prevents direct contact of the ice pack with the medicines.

You must also protect veterinary medicines from freezing. Although practices usually monitor cold chain products, refrigeration issues remain a common inspection finding.The type of refrigerator you use and the way you store products can significantly affect performance.

Common problems include poor cleaning, ice build-up, and overstocking, which can cause products to freeze when pushed against the fridge walls. Refrigerators should be cleaned regularly, not overfilled, and serviced routinely to ensure they operate correctly.
Keeping medicines away from your lunch
Credit: VMD
A common inspection finding is the storage of human food alongside veterinary medicines. Medicines and vaccine refrigerators must not be used for staff food.

We’ve  found items such as sandwiches, drinks, soup, butter, salad, and other food products in medicines fridges, creating a potential contamination risk. If inspectors identify food contamination or inappropriate storage, they  may take action, including seizing or disposing of affected products.

Inspectors have the authority to seize veterinary medicinal products and Schedule 5 products such as additives and medicated feeds, if storage conditions may have compromised their safety or effectiveness. Schedule 5 products include additives, in-feed premixes, premixtures, intermediate products, and medicated feeds. Where storage standards are not met, these products may be removed from use.
How do I monitor temperatures?

We see a wide range of temperature monitoring devices, from basic minimum/maximum thermometers to advanced digital, data-logging, and smart monitoring systems with remote alerts. The key thing to remember is that whatever system you use used, you must able to accurately monitor temperatures, maintain records, and identify and manage any temperature excursions.

Digital min/max thermometers
At an absolute minimum, we recommend the use of a digital thermometer that displays:

This approach provides a clear overview of temperature control since the previous check and allows any excursions to be identified promptly.
Ambient storage

Recording max/min temperatures does not give you any indication of the duration of any excursion, so the practice cannot determine if the temperature spike occurred for a few minutes, a few hours or even longer. Without knowing the duration of the excursion it is impossible to determine the extent to which the medicines have been compromised.
Thermometers with remote sensors

Thermometers consisting of a main display unit with a cabled sensor probe can be used effectively for both ambient and refrigerated storage within a single unit. Where these are used for refrigerated storage, it is advisable to insulate the sensor to better mimic the packaging of the product. This reduces sensitivity to frequent door openings and provides a more representative reading of product temperature rather than air temperature alone.
Data loggers

You can use data loggers as an alternative to manual min/max thermometers, but you must set them up correctly to identify temperature excursions and generate alerts when temperatures fall outside acceptable limits. You should understand the manufacturer's instructions, device indicators, and the actions required when alerts occur.

For refrigerated storage, including vaccine and vehicle fridges, you should download and review data at least weekly. Recording intervals vary, but approximately every 15-30 minutes is generally recommended, providing sufficient detail without creating excessive data.
Although data loggers automate temperature recording, they do not replace daily checks. Staff must still confirm that devices are working correctly and that no alerts have been triggered.
Smart thermometers
Smart thermometers  use Bluetooth or Wi‑Fi technology to continuously record temperatures, with data accessible through an app or online platform.

When you configure these systems properly, they can provide automatic alerts if temperatures fall outside the required range, enabling prompt action. Before purchasing, ensure the system is suitable for your storage arrangements, connectivity, and staff availability to respond to alerts.
As with any temperature monitoring system, staff must understand how it works, what alerts mean, and the actions required when a temperature excursion occurs.
External monitoring services

Third-party monitoring services can install equipment, monitor temperatures remotely, and notify users of excursions, often by text or phone call. While these services can reduce workload, responsibility remains with the holder to respond to alerts, maintain records, and ensure they are available for inspection.
A good tip to help ensure you are taking accurate readings is choose a temperature monitoring system that is calibrated.

title: A Level and level 3 results 2026 at a glance: key trends and context for teachers

content.content: More than 880,000 A and AS Level results have been issued today to students in England, with another 221,000 results for vocational and technical qualifications.

These results open doors for students to move on to the next stage in their lives, whether that be university, employment or apprenticeships. And they serve as recognition of – and reward for – the effort and quality of work displayed by those students. I offer my congratulations to everyone receiving results today.
Here are some key details about today’s A Level and level 3 results
What are the trends behind the results?
This year’s results picture is one of stability.

Small changes in grade distributions year-on-year are normal. Looking across A Level subjects with large enough entries to compare meaningfully, most show only small movements up or down. Some rising, some falling, typically by less than a percentage point either way.
This kind of variation happens every year and largely reflects the different mix of students taking each subject. The standard of work required to gain a particular grade remains constant.

There are noteworthy patterns and trends in the popularity of subjects at A Level. Maths was the subject studied by more students than any other, accounting for about one in 8 of the A Level results released today. Maths A Level has increased in size as a proportion of entries in recent years, and that trend has continued this year. Further maths A Level too has again seen strong growth this year.
After maths, the most commonly-taken A Level subjects were psychology and biology – the same as in 2025 – and chemistry and economics complete this year’s top 5.
The popularity of maths at A Level means outcomes have a significant effect on national trends.

The very small rise in the proportion of students achieving A* or A at A Level overall (from 28.2% in 2025 to 28.3% this year) has been largely driven by a small increase in those grades in maths (from 41.6% in 2025 to 42.1% this year).
The standard of work required to achieve any grade in maths this year was the same as previous years, so this rise reflects a slightly stronger cohort of students.
While subject level changes such as this are important, the overall national picture for A Level results in 2026 is one of stability.
What do I need to know about AS and A Level results?
What do I need to know about level 3 vocational and technical qualification results?
Where to find more details about A Level and level 3 results

Ofqual has published a statistical report on this year’s results. This is the place to go if you want more in-depth analysis of the results and outcomes for A Levels, AS, applied generals, tech levels and technical qualifications within T Levels.

We have also published interactive visualisations of level 3 results on Ofqual Analytics. This gives detailed breakdowns of outcomes according to types of school or college, by sex, for subject combinations, and more. This year is the first time you will be able to see results and subject uptake broken down geographically at local authority level.
Results day each August represents the culmination of hard work and commitment by students, teachers and many others. Congratulations to all students collecting their results this week.
Amanda Swann, Executive Director for Delivery, Ofqual

title: How the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary supported my journey, by Grace

content.content: My name is Grace, and I am currently completing a Customer Service Practitioner Level 2 apprenticeship with Ginger Nut Training after progressing from a scholarship.

Before this, I didn’t even understand how a modern-day apprenticeship worked, let alone how much one could change my life. I’m now working as a Client Engagement Administrator, supporting employers and learners throughout their apprenticeship journey. At 20 years old, I’ve found a real sense of purpose in helping others access opportunities that can change their lives, just as mine was changed. Every day, I’m building new skills, growing in confidence, and proving to myself that my past doesn’t have to define my future.

Like many care leavers, I faced challenges that many young people don’t have to think about. Starting an apprenticeship is exciting, but it can also be financially difficult, especially when you’re transitioning into independence. Although I am earning a living wage, I still have to pay my own way. Including rent, bills, saving and making arrangements to spend quality time with my siblings.
How the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary helped me

I first found out about the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary through my job role, working for a training provider and training under them. The process of accessing it was well explained and very straightforward for me, I felt supported throughout. Knowing that this funding was available made me feel that care leavers were being recognised and given support to succeed, rather than being expected to overcome every challenge on our own.
I decided to use my payments of the bursary towards buying my first car, and I can honestly say it has been one of the best decisions I have ever made.

Having a car has completely changed my experience. The impact has gone far beyond simply having transport. Owning a car has given me confidence and independence. It has allowed me to become more self-sufficient and has opened up opportunities that may not have been possible otherwise.

For me, the bursary wasn’t just financial support. It was an investment in my future. It removed one of the barriers that could have made completing my apprenticeship much more difficult and helped me build a stronger foundation for my career.

The opportunities I've had have been incredible. I've spoken in Parliament about improving apprenticeship opportunities for care leavers, been invited to speak on panels and at national events to share my experiences and been recognised as a finalist for Apprentice of the Year. I was also proud to become an ambassador in a role that promotes helping youth into work.

It's amazing to see how far I've come. My apprenticeship has given me much more than qualifications, it has given me confidence, purpose and the belief that I can achieve things I once thought were out of reach. I'm now excited to continue my journey by progressing onto a higher-level apprenticeship, building on everything I've learned so far and continuing to develop both personally and professionally.
My advice to other care leavers, employers and training providers

My advice to other care leavers is simple - don't be afraid to ask about the support that is available. I know it can sometimes feel like you're expected to manage everything on your own, but the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary exists because people recognise that care leavers may face additional challenges.

Taking advantage of that support isn't a weakness, it's giving yourself the best possible chance to succeed. I also think it should be said that it doesn’t have to be used in the same way as I did, while having a car is a huge achievement for me, having a pot of money to support any finances and take away worries is just as huge of an achievement.

I would also encourage employers and training providers to actively promote the bursary. There may be care leavers who don't realise they are entitled to it, and something as simple as telling them about the funding could make a life changing difference. Whether it helps someone pay for travel, buy equipment, or gain greater independence like it did for me, the impact can last long after the apprenticeship has finished.
Unfortunately, the bursary remains underclaimed, meaning too many eligible care leavers are missing out on support that could make a real difference to their lives.

If you're a care leaver thinking about an apprenticeship, ask your training provider about the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary and what support is available. It could be the helping hand that makes all the difference, just as it did for me.  Employers and training providers, make sure your apprentices know about the bursary. Training providers claim on behalf of apprentices.
See guidance here: Apprenticeships care leavers’ bursary guidance - GOV.UK

title: Managing farms and land during prolonged dry weather and drought

content.content: Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought after experiencing record-low rainfall and unusually high temperatures.
So far in August, rainfall has been 5% of the seasonal average, following the driest July in 190 years.

This summer has been hard for farmers. Dry conditions are placing pressure on farm businesses. Grass growth has reduced, forage is less available, crops are being affected and water supplies are under pressure. Farmers are also facing higher fertiliser and red diesel costs because of the conflict in the Middle East.
Food security is national security, which is why we are working closely with farmers, the Environment Agency and the water sector during this exceptionally dry weather.

Defra met with farming and food representatives on Wednesday 5 August to discuss solutions to the challenges the dry weather presents. The National Drought Group met on Monday 10 August and will continue to co-ordinate the broader impacts of dry weather.

We are looking at how we can support farmers through this prolonged dry weather and hope to be able to say more on this soon, alongside how we're building greater long-term resilience to climate shocks.
In this blog post, we've gathered information and resources to help farmers and growers understand what support is available and what steps you can take now.
Access to water
Environment Agency guidance on abstraction and irrigation
If prolonged dry weather is affecting your access to water, there may be options available to help you.
Colleagues at the Environment Agency have published a dedicated blog bringing together drought advice, abstraction updates and useful resources for farmers and growers on the following:
The Environment Agency can advise farmers on measures available during drought. These include options that sit outside usual abstraction licence conditions.
If you have any questions, you can call their National Customer Contact Centre for advice on 03708 506 506.
Managing reservoirs
Extreme weather can impact the safety of your reservoir.
During periods of drought, regularly check reservoir levels and inspect embankments, spillways and surrounding areas for signs of cracking or damage caused by dry ground conditions.
It’s also important to manage vegetation and reduce fire risks around reservoirs and infrastructure.
Further advice is available on GOV.UK on how to manage, maintain and improve your reservoir in extreme weather.
Storage of flammable materials
High temperatures and prolonged dry weather can increase the fire risk for hay, straw and other materials.

Where possible, move hay and straw into storage promptly after harvest, ensuring that moisture levels are sufficiently low. Damp hay can generate heat as it dries, creating a risk of spontaneous combustion.
Sections 2 and 4 of the NFU's Risk Management Programme for the Prevention of Fires on Farms sets this out in further detail.

Where possible, keep hay and straw storage away from other farm buildings, particularly those which house fuel, fertiliser, chemicals or other combustible materials. Try to leave adequate space between stacks where possible.
Devon and Somerset's Fire and Rescue Service have created this page on monitoring hay and straw temperatures.
Animal health & welfare
Hot, dry weather can place additional pressure on the health and wellbeing of livestock and increase demand for water.
Make sure animals have sufficient drinking water, check them regularly for signs of heat stress, and have their management or diets adjusted if necessary.
It’s also worth planning ahead for potential water shortages, identifying alternative water sources, and where required, planning arrangements to move animals.
Visit GOV.UK for more advice on caring for farm animals and horses in extreme weather.
Wildfire & creating firebreaks
Mitigating fire risks

Many parts of the country are at a very high or exceptional risk of fire. You can check to see the fire risk in your area in these Fire Severity Index (FSI) maps, provided by the Met Office, for the whole of England and Wales.

This Farmland Safety and Fire Prevention booklet produced by the Fire & Rescue services, in partnership with the NFU, examines the fire dangers which are commonly found on farms. It identifies simple ways in which risks can be reduced.
Creating firebreaks
In areas facing a high risk of wildfire, creating firebreaks can help limit the spread of fire and protect livestock, farm equipment, homes, and crops where they have not already been harvested.

Firebreaks are created by removing or managing flammable vegetation, such as long, dry grass. This can include cutting, clearing or ploughing. Reducing vegetation limits the fuel available to a fire and helps contain it. It also exposes bare soil that flames cannot easily cross.

To be effective, the width of the firebreak should be around 3 times the height of the highest crop or vegetation next to it. For example, if your wheat crop is around 1 metre high, the firebreak would be around 3 metres wide as a minimum.
If you’re considering creating a firebreak, make sure you comply with all relevant law and regulatory requirements which apply to you and your land.

If your land is in an Environmental Land Management (ELM) revenue agreement, you must contact the RPA before you create a firebreak on that land. Read the ‘ELM revenue schemes’ information below to find out how to do this.
Controlled burning of heather, grassland and crop residue
In areas that are suffering from extended periods of dry weather, undertaking routine controlled burning significantly increases the likelihood of a wildfire starting.

For the safety of your local community, Defra is advising farmers to not burn heather, rough grass or other vegetation, even if you have a licence, consent or agreement that permits you to burn at this time of year.
Farmers and land owners should continue to work with the Fire & Rescue Service who, in the event of a live incident, may undertake tactical burns to create a fuel break.
Schemes and grants
ELM revenue schemes
We recognise that prolonged hot and dry weather can create challenges for farmers and land managers delivering actions under our ELM revenue schemes.
We are actively considering whether we need to make temporary adjustments to ELM revenue agreements under the following schemes:
We will provide a further update on any temporary adjustments as soon as possible.
In the meantime, if extreme weather prevents you from meeting your ELM agreement requirements, you must tell the RPA:
The RPA will use the information you provide to decide what action to take. If there is any impact on your payments they will tell you the outcome of any decisions in writing.
Innovation & technology
Through the Farming Innovation Programme, we’re supporting farmers to implement innovative technologies that help use water more efficiently.

Trying something new can involve time, cost and uncertainty. Grants like the Accelerating Development of Practices and Technologies (ADOPT) fund helps reduce that risk by funding practical, on-farm trials and demonstrations led by farmers.
This includes projects trialling new technologies for conserving water on farm, such as this smart irrigation trial led by Water Resources East.
ADOPT has a rolling application window, you can find out how to apply by visiting the Innovate UK website.
Local Resource Option Screening Studies

We launched the latest round of Local Resource Option (LRO) Screening Studies earlier this summer. These studies support groups of farmers to identify practical solutions to improve long-term water resilience.
The application window for 2026/27 is now closed and projects selected.

However, if you would like to be considered on a first-come-first-served basis (subject to eligibility criteria), we may be able to offer further projects. This could happen if funds remain after the currently selected projects are awarded to contractors.
Please contact WRAgriculture@environment-agency.gov.uk for more information.
Further Information
Subscribe to the Defra Farming Blog to be the first to find out further information on guidance and support for managing your farm through periods of drought.
By subscribing, you’ll receive an email whenever a new post is published.

title: How does the Environment Agency manage abstraction to protect the environment?

content.content: Water is essential for drinking, farming, industry, wildlife and recreation. Managing our rivers, lakes, estuaries, wetlands and groundwater properly ensures the needs of society, the economy and nature can be met over the long term.
2026 has seen the driest July in 190 years, with just 5 per cent of expected rainfall.

This has placed significant demands on abstraction, particularly for irrigation, and agricultural reservoir stocks have declined rapidly, especially where abstractors rely heavily on storage. If you own, operate or are planning to build a reservoir, our new planning guides explain the requirements.

Sustainable water abstraction is essential to ensure that river flows and groundwater levels support ecology and natural resilience. We work with abstractors to balance the needs of the public, industry, farmers and the environment.
What are abstraction licences?

Abstraction is the process of taking water from a river, lake or groundwater source for uses such as irrigation, industry, recreation or drinking water. The Environment Agency grants abstraction licences to protect the environment and the rights of existing lawful water users.
Those with abstraction licences are allowed to take water in line with the conditions of their licence.

Abstracting more than 20 cubic metres a day generally requires a licence, though some activities, such as firefighting, are exempt. If you take water from the same source at multiple points, the combined total must be 20 cubic metres or less a day to qualify for exemption.

If you don't hold a licence, you may be able to agree a trade or share with an existing licence holder, permanently or temporarily, provided all licence conditions can still be met. Where an abstraction is moved to a different abstraction point, the buyer of the abstraction right would normally have to apply for their own licence or change their existing licence if they have one.
Not all activities require an abstraction licence to take place with some being exempt.
Abstraction licence holders can manage their accounts online to see a summary of their licence and past returns.
How can the Environment Agency restrict abstraction?
There are two main types of restrictions that the Environment Agency can implement on abstractors at times of pressure: hands-off flow conditions and Section 57 restrictions.

Hands-off flow conditions on licences reduce or prevent abstraction to protect other abstractors and the environment. Many of these restrictions have come into effect in 2026 due to very low river flows. Licence holders who have hands-off flow condition on their licences will be notified when the condition comes into force, with as much advance notice as possible.
Section 57 of the Water Resources Act 1991 allows formal notices to be issued to holders of spray irrigation abstraction licences to protect river flows during drought throughout a catchment.
Spray irrigation abstraction licence holders can help make the most of the water which their licence authorises to take by:
Environment Agency updated prospects for irrigation report for summer 2026 can be found on gov.uk.

We work closely with farmers, the National Farmers Union (NFU), Water Abstraction Groups (WAGs) and Internal Drainage Boards (IDBs) to give as much advanced notice as possible before cessation conditions are needed on abstraction licences to protect the environment.
We continue to carry out irrigation patrols and other compliance checks to ensure all abstractors are complying with their licence conditions to help protect water availability.

If abstractors believe that they may not be able to comply with their abstraction licence or have issues accessing water supplies, they should contact their local area office for further advice as soon as possible.
What support is available for those with abstraction licences who may have restrictions in place?
General guidance is available for abstraction licence holders affected by prolonged dry weather and drought, alongside short and long-term options to improve water access and resilience.

It's free and open 24 hours a day.

title: Can technology improve people’s experience of organisational change?

content.content: Change is a human challenge

In the Civil Service, organisational change is a reality. Teams evolve, priorities shift, and departments periodically go through restructures, machinery of government changes, and workforce redesign programmes. While each change programme is different, they all have one thing in common: they affect people.

Change is ultimately a human challenge. It impacts careers, wellbeing, and confidence in the organisation. Technology cannot solve those challenges, but it can support the processes around them by making them more transparent, consistent and fair.

I became involved in a large organisational restructure because the allocation process presented exactly that kind of opportunity. The restructure involved allocating a large number of people across multiple grades, limited vacancies and competing preferences, all within a complex set of agreed business rules. Managing this fairly and consistently through a manual process was increasingly difficult. The challenge was not simply to make the process faster, but to reduce risk and give people greater confidence in the outcome.
The experience reinforced an important lesson: when technology is used in people-focused decisions, transparency and accountability must come before sophistication.
The challenge of organisational restructure

The existing allocation process involved significant manual effort. Candidates could express preferences across multiple roles, vacancies were limited, and allocations needed to consider scores, preferences and redeployment rules simultaneously.
Managing this process manually created several challenges, including:
Most importantly, long processing times meant people spent longer waiting for clarity about their future roles.
The objective was therefore not simply operational efficiency. It was to reduce the risks associated with complex manual processing to improve outcomes for the people involved.
Using technology to support (not replace) decision making
At the heart of the solution was an allocation algorithm that matched candidates to roles.
The word "algorithm" can sometimes imply automated decision-making. In this case, the system acted more like a transparent administrative process than an AI model.
The algorithm was “deterministic”, which meant it followed a defined sequence of rules:

Importantly, the system did not learn, predict or optimise like an AI model. It simply applied the agreed rules consistently and at scale. Every allocation could be traced back to documented rules and independently verified.
Choosing automation over artificial intelligence was a deliberate choice to ensure:
Ethics and governance
Governance and ethical oversight were built into the project from the outset.
Alongside HR and trade union engagement, we worked with the departmental ethics committee to review the proposed approach.

The allocation process was never intended to replace human judgement. Cases that could not be resolved automatically were escalated for review. Decision-makers retained the ability to challenge or override outcomes where there was a clear and documented rationale.
This early engagement helped shape both the design and the governance framework, while keeping stakeholders informed of the benefits of the approach prior to implementation.
Testing and assurance
Before deployment, we ran the allocation process in parallel with the existing manual method.
This allowed us to:
The comparison demonstrated that the automated approach produced consistent and explainable outcomes while dramatically reducing processing time.
Impact
The system reduced a process that previously took days to complete to a matter of seconds. But its most important benefits were not technical.

For the people involved, this meant less time waiting for clarity during an uncertain period. For decision-makers, it created a transparent, auditable record of every allocation, reduced the working hours needed to complete the process, and made each decision easier to explain.

The manual method used for comparison produced several errors that the algorithm did not. There was only one instance where the human reviewer overrode the algorithm’s output: allocating someone their second choice freed up their first-choice role for an unallocated candidate.
The experience shows that government organisations do not always need advanced AI to solve complex problems.
What’s next?
There are clear lessons for organisational change across government.

Many workforce and organisational challenges involve large volumes of information, complex business rules and significant consequences for individuals. These are exactly the situations where well-designed automation can add value.

The approach is also highly replicable. Because the solution relies on documented business rules rather than specialist AI models, it can be adapted by other departments facing similar allocation or prioritisation challenges.
Successful change is about improving outcomes for people. This can be supported with technology by involving users and ethics committees from the beginning.
Conclusion

If there is one takeaway from this work, it is that technology should make important decisions easier to understand, not harder.  You do not always need AI to solve complex public-sector problems. Well-designed automation can support decision making while remaining understandable and auditable.

For organisations that feel cautious about using technology in sensitive decisions, the lesson is simple: start with explainability. People’s confidence in your solution will grow when they can understand how the system works, challenge its outputs and see that human judgement remains part of the process.
If you would like to know more about the algorithm or would like advice on replicating our work, please reach out in the comments.

title: How we’re helping people and businesses get help from APHA with sustainable design

content.content: Senior content designer Eleanor Shakeshaft and senior service designer Ibarieze Abani from the APHA improving customer experience team discuss how they’re improving the way customers get support when they can't find the answers they need online.

In our team’s first blog post, we explained our choice of tools and technology. Here, we zoom in further to look at how workshopping with colleagues in customer service teams has been instrumental in shaping how we build a more sustainable service.
To recap, our team’s goals are to:
Simplifying the journey to get help
When customers need support from APHA, there are two steps in their journey:
Historically, these journeys could be difficult to navigate. Customers were often presented with long lists of email addresses and contact routes, leaving them to decide which team could help.

65% of APHA's customer emails were sent to the wrong team and needed to be redirected. This was a poor experience for customers who had to wait longer for a reply and was an inefficient use of time for CSC teams.
To address this, we've focused on both stages of the experience.
Helping customers find the right team
One of the main entry points for users needing support is the page previously known as Contact APHA.
This page is now titled Get help with animal and plant health. We renamed it because research showed this wording was more intuitive to users.
We're also testing a user-centred routing tool that helps people find the right team based on what they're trying to do.
It uses familiar language and does the hard work of getting customers to the right team, instead of expecting them to understand APHA's internal structure.
This makes it quicker and easier for customers to get the help they need.
Making it easier to get in touch
The biggest change to customers is replacing many of APHA's email addresses with contact forms.
Moving away from email to contact forms and a Contact Centre as a Service (CCaaS) platform has several benefits, including:
However, delivering this change at scale presented a challenge.
A large number of services and contact routes were in scope. We needed a way to design and roll out forms at pace, without creating entirely bespoke solutions for every team.
Learning from a pilot approach
We started with a pilot in Alpha, working closely with two service areas: pet travel and customer advice.
This allowed us to:
The pilot approach gave us valuable insight into how different teams worked. But it quickly became clear it wouldn't be an efficient way to deliver contact forms at scale.
The early forms were highly tailored to individual services. This required significant collaboration and refinement to accommodate complex policy needs.
We also discovered many CSC teams handle a broader range of work than expected, including specialist applications and processes.
Stepping back to see the bigger picture
To create a more scalable solution, we took a step back and looked across the wider CSC landscape.
Through workshops with teams, we explored:
This helped us move from designing individual forms to designing a reusable pattern.
We combined the insights from these workshops with a set of design principles and practical constraints. For example, limiting the number of fields in the first iteration of a form.
The end result was a contact form pattern that could be applied across multiple services,
Taking this approach has allowed us to co-design with teams and publish forms more efficiently and sustainable, without compromising on quality and consistency for customers.
A pattern in action: reporting a farm animal welfare concern
One example of this approach can be seen in the 'Report a farm animal welfare concern' service.

Although this service sits slightly outside the scope of the wider ‘getting help’ work, it is an important priority area for APHA. Given the scope and timelines, designing a service entirely from scratch wasn't practical.
Instead, we looked at other similar Defra services to identify patterns we could reuse.
Patterns gave us:
Rather than reinventing the wheel, we were able to build on existing good practice and focus our effort on aspects unique to the service.
Designing for the future
This work is about more than replacing inboxes with forms.

We’re adding patterns and components like this to the Defra Digital service manual to be reused by other teams. This will reduce the time and resources needed to design from scratch for similar services.
This approach supports Defra's ambitions to invest in reusable products and common platforms, rather than creating one-off solutions for individual programmes.
This will enable us to improve user experience, scale delivery, reduce duplication and improve consistency across Defra.
